definition:
Salvation is God's rescue of human beings from sin and its consequences (guilt, bondage, alienation from God, death, and judgment) into restored life with him, a rescue that Scripture says reaches in the end to the renewal of the whole creation. The Christian church confesses that this salvation is God's own work in Jesus Christ, received as a gift of grace through faith and not earned by human merit: “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9). Scripture describes the one salvation through many pictures, each of which has its own study here: justification (being declared right with God by the judge), redemption (being bought out of slavery), reconciliation (enemies made friends), adoption (strangers made children and heirs), new birth (the dead made alive), union with Christ, sanctification (being made holy), and final glory. This study traces the whole; the site's page on how we are saved sets out at length how Reformed, Arminian, and other traditions understand the relation of God's grace to the human will.

The Hebrew vocabulary centers on the verb yasha', usually in the form hoshia', ‘to save, deliver, help, give victory’, which occurs about two hundred times, and its nouns yeshu'ah and yesha', ‘salvation, deliverance, victory’. The words are concrete: to be saved is to be brought out of a tight place, whether from enemies, sickness, oppression, or sin. The names Joshua and Jesus (Hebrew Yehoshua, shortened to Yeshua) are built on the same root and are usually understood as ‘the LORD saves’ or ‘the LORD is salvation’, which is why the angel says, “you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Other words fill out the picture: ga'al, ‘to redeem’ as a kinsman buys back a relative, and padah, ‘to ransom’. The Greek verb sōzō, ‘to save, rescue, keep safe, heal’, appears about a hundred times in the New Testament, with the nouns sōtēria, ‘salvation’, and sōtēr, ‘savior’. Its range matters: when Jesus tells a woman, “your faith has healed you” (Mark 5:34), and another, “Your faith has saved you” (Luke 7:50), the same verb stands behind both. Grace translates the Hebrew chen, ‘favor’ (first in Genesis 6:8, where Noah “found favor in the eyes of the LORD”), and is closely related to chesed, God's covenant love, which the Berean Standard Bible renders ‘loving devotion’. In the New Testament the word is charis, ‘favor freely given’, a gift that by definition cannot be earned: “if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace” (Romans 11:6).
ot:
The Old Testament tells salvation as a story before it states it as a doctrine. After the first sin, God pronounces judgment but also promises that the woman's seed will crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15), and he clothes the man and woman himself (Genesis 3:21). When the earth is filled with violence, “Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8): grace comes first in the story, and the ark is God's means of carrying a remnant through judgment. God calls Abram so that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3), and when Abram trusts God's promise of a son, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), the verse Paul will make the charter of justification by faith. The word yeshu'ah first appears in the dying Jacob's prayer, “I await Your salvation, O LORD” (Genesis 49:18).

The exodus is the Old Testament's great picture of salvation, the event to which Israel looked back as the psalms and prophets looked forward. At the sea Moses tells the people, “Stand firm and you will see the LORD's salvation, which He will accomplish for you today” (Exodus 14:13), and on the far shore they sing, “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation” (Exodus 15:2). The order of events is theological. God redeems Israel from slavery first, and only then gives the law, which begins, “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Obedience answers rescue; it does not purchase it. Deuteronomy insists that God did not choose Israel because they were many but “because the LORD loved you” (Deuteronomy 7:8). The Passover lamb, whose blood marked the houses the destroyer passed over, and the sacrificial system given at Sinai taught that sin is deadly and that God provides the means of covering it (see the study on sacrifice and atonement). In the wilderness, those bitten by serpents lived by looking to the bronze serpent God told Moses to lift up (Numbers 21:8-9), an image Jesus will apply to his own lifting up (John 3:14-15).

In the land, God repeatedly raises up deliverers: when Israel cried out, God raised up Othniel “as a deliverer to save them” (Judges 3:9, which uses both moshia', ‘deliverer’, and hoshia', ‘to save’). The psalms turn salvation into prayer and praise. “Salvation belongs to the LORD” (Psalm 3:8) is the confession of a king fleeing his son. The psalmists ask to be saved from enemies, illness, and death, and increasingly from sin itself: David prays, “Create in me a clean heart, O God” and “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation” (Psalm 51:10, 12), and another psalm confesses, “If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness” (Psalm 130:3-4). The psalmists know that God “has not dealt with us according to our sins” (Psalm 103:10).

The prophets deepen and widen the hope. Israel's sin brings exile, and the prophets promise a new exodus in which God will save his people from their sins as well as their captors. God declares, “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me” (Isaiah 43:11), and the salvation reaches past Israel: “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22). The servant is to bring God's salvation “to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6), and he will do it by suffering: “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). The invitation is free: “you without money, come, buy, and eat” (Isaiah 55:1). Jeremiah promises a new covenant with the law written on the heart and sins remembered no more (Jeremiah 31:33-34), and Ezekiel a new heart and God's own Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26-27). Joel promises that “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved” (Joel 2:32), Jonah confesses from the belly of the fish, “Salvation is from the LORD!” (Jonah 2:9), and Habakkuk hears that “the righteous will live by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4), where the Hebrew 'emunah means steady faithfulness grounded in trust. Salvation in the Old Testament is mostly about life in this world, among God's people, in the land. But by its last books the horizon has opened beyond death: Daniel sees that many who sleep in the dust “will awake, some to everlasting life” (Daniel 12:2).
nt:
The Gospels open with salvation arriving in a person. The child will be called Jesus “because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21); Mary rejoices in “God my Savior” (Luke 1:47); the aged Simeon, holding the infant, says, “my eyes have seen Your salvation” (Luke 2:30). Jesus' ministry enacts it. He heals the sick, casts out demons, and forgives sins, and the Gospels use the same verb for being made well and being saved. He eats with tax collectors and sinners, tells of a father who runs to his returning son (Luke 15:20), and says that the tax collector who prayed, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner”, went home justified rather than the Pharisee (Luke 18:13-14). At Zacchaeus's house he announces, “Today salvation has come to this house” and states his mission: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:9-10). He gives his life “as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). John's Gospel speaks of salvation as eternal life, the life of the age to come begun now: “For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16), and that life is to know the Father and the Son (John 17:3).

The apostles preach salvation through Jesus alone and by grace. Peter tells the council, “Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12); when a jailer asks, “what must I do to be saved?” Paul and Silas answer, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved” (Acts 16:30-31); and at the Jerusalem council, deciding that Gentile believers need not be circumcised, Peter says, “it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are” (Acts 15:11). Paul gives the fullest account. The gospel is “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16), because “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Romans 3:23-24). Wages are owed, but a gift is free: “the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23). God showed his love in that “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Salvation is received by calling on the Lord in faith: “if you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). Titus 3:5 gathers the themes: “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.”

The New Testament speaks of salvation in three tenses. Believers have been saved (Ephesians 2:8 uses a Greek perfect participle, sesōsmenoi, for a completed act with lasting effect); they are being saved (“to us who are being saved it is the power of God”, 1 Corinthians 1:18); and they will be saved, “saved from wrath through Him” at the judgment (Romans 5:9), since “our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed” (Romans 13:11). Paul's chain in Romans 8:29-30 runs from God's foreknowing through predestining, calling, and justifying to glorifying, and the salvation it describes reaches the body and the cosmos: creation itself “will be set free from its bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21). Grace does not leave people as they were. The same passage that excludes works as the ground of salvation says that believers are “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:10); Paul tells the Philippians to “work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act” (Philippians 2:12-13); grace “instructs us to renounce ungodliness” (Titus 2:12). James warns that “faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead” (James 2:17), and most interpreters hold that James and Paul address different questions: Paul, the ground on which a sinner is accepted; James, the kind of faith that is real. Paul's own phrase is “faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6).

The later letters and Revelation keep the future in view. Hebrews warns against neglecting “such a great salvation” (Hebrews 2:3) and says Christ “will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him” (Hebrews 9:28). Peter blesses God who has given “new birth into a living hope” and speaks of believers “shielded by God's power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time” (1 Peter 1:3, 5). In Revelation a multitude from every nation cries, “Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10), and the story ends where salvation was always heading: God dwelling with his people, wiping away every tear, with “no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4).

keyTexts.why: Abram believes the LORD's promise and it is credited to him as righteousness. Paul's charter for salvation received by faith (Romans 4).
Israel is told to stand firm and see the LORD's salvation at the sea. The exodus becomes the Bible's pattern for God's saving acts.
The law begins by recalling redemption from slavery. Obedience answers God's saving act; it does not earn it.
No one could stand if God kept a record of sins, but with him there is forgiveness. Salvation from sin as well as from enemies.
God calls all the ends of the earth to turn to him and be saved. The one Savior's salvation is offered to the nations.
The servant is pierced for our transgressions and by his wounds we are healed. The prophets' deepest picture of how God saves.
God promises cleansing, a new heart, and his Spirit within. Salvation as inner renewal, not only outward rescue.
Jesus is named because he will save his people from their sins. The name itself announces salvation.
Salvation comes to Zacchaeus's house, and Jesus says he came to seek and save the lost. Grace that goes looking for sinners.
The Son is lifted up like the bronze serpent so that whoever believes has eternal life. God sent him to save, not to condemn.
There is salvation in no one else. The apostles' confession of Christ as the only Savior.
All have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by God's grace through redemption in Christ. The heart of Paul's gospel.
God's saving purpose runs from foreknowledge to glory, and nothing can separate believers from his love.
The dead are made alive with Christ, saved by grace through faith, not by works, and created for good works.
God saved us not by our righteous deeds but by his mercy, through new birth and the Spirit, so that justified by grace we become heirs.

history:
The earliest Christian writers proclaimed salvation through Christ's death and resurrection without defining its mechanics, and they joined grace and holy living closely. The first great controversy about grace came in the early fifth century. Pelagius, a British monk teaching in Rome, and his follower Celestius held that human beings, created good, are able to obey God's commands, so that grace chiefly means God's gifts of free will, the law, and Christ's example and forgiveness. Augustine of Hippo answered in a long series of treatises from about 411 until his death in 430 that sin has bound the human will, so that God's grace must go before, free, and accompany the will in every good act, including the first movement of faith. The Council of Carthage in 418 condemned Pelagian teaching, Pope Zosimus endorsed its judgment, and the Council of Ephesus in 431 condemned Celestius. A middle position, later called semi-Pelagianism and associated with John Cassian and Faustus of Riez, held that the beginning of faith could come from the human side with grace following; the Second Council of Orange (529), led by Caesarius of Arles, rejected this and taught that even the beginning of faith is a gift of grace, while also rejecting the idea that God predestines anyone to evil.

The medieval West kept Augustine's insistence on grace while developing a detailed account of how grace is given through the sacraments, heals the soul as an infused gift, and enables works that God rewards. By the late Middle Ages, some theologians taught that God gives grace to those who do what is in them, and it was against this that Martin Luther reacted. His discovery that the righteousness of God in Romans 1:17 is the righteousness God gives to faith became the center of the Reformation, confessed in the Augsburg Confession (1530, Article IV): people are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith, not by their own strength or merits. The Council of Trent, in its Decree on Justification (Session 6, 1547), affirmed that salvation begins with God's prevenient grace, that no one can merit the grace of justification, and that faith is the beginning of salvation, while rejecting justification by faith alone understood as trust alone and teaching that justification includes the inner renewal of the person and that grace can be increased and lost. Protestants divided among themselves over grace and the will: the Remonstrants (1610) followed Jacobus Arminius in teaching conditional election and resistible grace, and the Synod of Dort (1618-1619) answered with its Canons, which became the source of the later five-point summary of Calvinism. John Wesley's experience at Aldersgate Street in London on 24 May 1738, when he felt he trusted Christ alone for salvation, launched a revival that joined Arminian theology to an emphasis on assurance and holiness. Eastern Orthodox theology, which did not pass through the Pelagian or Reformation controversies in the same way, has described salvation chiefly as theosis, participation in the divine life through union with Christ (2 Peter 1:4), with human freedom cooperating with grace.

The modern period brought both new divisions and new agreements. Nineteenth-century liberal theology often reframed salvation as moral and religious development; the Social Gospel movement, articulated by Walter Rauschenbusch in A Theology for the Social Gospel (1917), stressed the salvation of social structures; and twentieth-century evangelicals reasserted personal conversion, while the Lausanne Covenant (1974) affirmed both evangelism and social responsibility as parts of Christian duty, with evangelism primary. The Second Vatican Council (Lumen Gentium 16, 1964) taught that those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel but seek God sincerely and try to do his will may attain salvation, always through Christ. On 31 October 1999 the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, confessing together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit, we are accepted by God and receive the Spirit who renews our hearts. The World Methodist Council affirmed it in 2006 and the World Communion of Reformed Churches in 2017. The differences that remain are real, but every major Christian tradition confesses that salvation is God's gracious work in Christ.

differ.view: Grace and the human will: who takes the first step?
differ.body: Reformed (Calvinist) theology holds that sinners are spiritually dead and cannot turn to God until God regenerates them; God's electing grace effectively brings the elect to faith, so that salvation is God's work from first to last (Ephesians 2:1-9; John 6:44). Arminian and Wesleyan theology holds that sinners are equally helpless in themselves, but that God gives a prevenient (‘going before’) grace to all people, freeing the will to accept or resist the gospel, because God desires all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4). Provisionists, found especially among Southern Baptists, hold that the gospel itself, preached in the Spirit's power, enables hearers to respond, without a separate prior grace. All affirm that salvation is by grace and that no one can boast. The site's page on how we are saved sets out each view in its own defenders' words, and the studies on election and on God's sovereignty and human choice trace the texts.

differ.view: How is grace received: faith alone, or faith with the sacraments and the life of the church?
differ.body: Protestant churches teach that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone, on account of Christ alone; good works and the sacraments follow as fruit and as means by which God strengthens faith, but they are not part of the ground of acceptance. The Catholic Church teaches that grace comes first and cannot be merited, that faith is the beginning and root of salvation, and that God ordinarily gives justifying grace through baptism and renews it through the sacraments, with grace-enabled cooperation and growth in holiness belonging to justification itself. Orthodox churches speak of salvation as a lifelong participation in God through the church's sacramental life, in which divine grace and human freedom work together (synergy), without a separate forensic moment at the center. The studies on justification, new birth, union with Christ, and baptism and the Lord's Supper treat these differences in detail.

differ.view: What of those who never hear the gospel?
differ.body: Many evangelical and Reformed theologians, Ronald Nash among recent writers, hold that explicit faith in Christ is necessary for salvation, pointing to Acts 4:12, John 14:6, and Romans 10:13-15, where Paul asks how people can believe in one of whom they have not heard; this conviction has driven much missionary sacrifice. Inclusivists, including Clark Pinnock (A Wideness in God's Mercy, 1992) and John Sanders (No Other Name, 1992), hold that salvation is only through Christ's work but that some who have never heard of him may be saved by responding in faith to the light God gives, as Old Testament believers such as Melchizedek, Job, and Cornelius before Peter came (Acts 10) did; the Catholic Church's teaching in Lumen Gentium 16 is similar. Others hold that Scripture does not answer the question and that it must be left to the judgment of a God who is just and merciful, while the church obeys the command to preach. All affirm that Christ is the only Savior.

Many evangelicals hold that salvation is first and chiefly reconciliation of sinners to God and deliverance from judgment, with care for the poor and work for justice as the fruit and companion of the gospel but not part of salvation itself; the Lausanne Covenant (1974) called evangelism primary while affirming social responsibility. Advocates of integral mission, among them the Latin American evangelicals René Padilla and Samuel Escobar, hold that the salvation Jesus announced (Luke 4:18-19) addresses the whole person and community, so that word and deed cannot be ranked. Liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez (A Theology of Liberation, 1971) have spoken of salvation as including God's liberation of the poor from oppression; the Catholic Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, in instructions of 1984 and 1986, affirmed the church's concern for liberation while criticizing elements drawn from Marxist analysis. All agree that the salvation Scripture promises reaches finally to the renewal of creation (Romans 8:21).

errors:
The church has rejected teachings that make salvation a human achievement. Pelagianism, condemned at Carthage (418) and Ephesus (431), held that people can obey God without the grace that frees the will; semi-Pelagianism, rejected at Orange (529), held that people can make the first move toward God. Both deny that salvation is grace from its beginning. The Galatian error Paul opposed, requiring Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the law in order to belong, has returned in many forms, whenever a church adds its own requirements to faith in Christ as a condition of acceptance with God (Galatians 1:6; 2:16). Its mirror image is antinomianism, the claim that because salvation is free, obedience does not matter; Paul anticipated it (“Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not!”, Romans 6:1-2), Luther opposed it when Johann Agricola denied that the law should be preached to Christians in the 1530s, and Dietrich Bonhoeffer described its modern form in Discipleship (1937) as cheap grace, forgiveness preached without repentance and discipleship.

Two popular distortions shrink salvation. One is the therapeutic reduction that the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton named moralistic therapeutic deism (Soul Searching, 2005): God wants people to be nice and feel good about themselves and will take good people to heaven, so that sin, the cross, and grace drop out. The other is prosperity teaching, which presents salvation as the promise of health and wealth to those with enough faith, turning grace into a transaction and suffering into a sign of failure. The New Testament's salvation is greater than both: rescue from sin and death through a crucified Savior, with glory promised at the end of a road that often runs through suffering (Romans 8:17-18).
life:
Because salvation is a gift, a believer's standing with God does not rise and fall with their performance. The tax collector who could only say “God, have mercy on me, a sinner” went home justified, and the same mercy is open to anyone. That frees people from the exhausting work of proving themselves, and it removes the ground for looking down on others, since no one can boast (Ephesians 2:9). It also means that failure is not the end: Christians confess their sins to a God who has already dealt with them in Christ.

Because salvation has three tenses, the Christian life holds together rest and effort. Believers rest in what God has done, work out what he is working in them, and wait with hope for what he will finish (Philippians 1:6). Salvation shapes prayer (thanksgiving for what has been given and trust for what is needed), shapes ethics (gratitude rather than fear as the motive for obedience), and shapes hope (not merely a soul escaping the world but a whole person raised and a creation set free). And because the salvation God gives is offered to “all the ends of the earth”, those who have received it are sent to announce it, in word and deed, to others.
questions: The law in Exodus 20 begins by reminding Israel that God had already rescued them. How does that order, rescue first and commands second, shape the way you understand obedience to God?
Scripture speaks of salvation in the past, present, and future tenses. Which of the three do you tend to forget, and what difference would it make to remember it?

Paul says salvation is not by works, yet believers are created for good works (Ephesians 2:8-10), and James says faith without works is dead. How would you explain the relationship to someone who has never read the Bible?
